stages.name: Conglomerate integration: advantages and disadvantages
stages.title: Conglomerate integration: advantages and disadvantages
stages.sub: After this, the student can explain why firms merge across unrelated markets, and the benefits and risks that follow.

steps.q: A biscuit maker merges with an insurance company. Do these two firms sell to the same market, using the same skills and supply chains?
steps.right: No, they operate in completely different markets
steps.wrong: Yes, they operate in the same market
steps.hint: Think about what biscuits and insurance actually have in common.
steps.pre: So the merged firm now operates across

steps.q: If the biscuit market suddenly slumps, does the insurance business, in a completely different market, also collapse?
steps.right: No, it can keep earning as normal
steps.hint: The two markets are unrelated. Does bad news in one usually hit the other?
steps.pre: So spreading into unrelated markets gives the firm

steps.q: The biscuit maker also owns a chain of cafés. Does it already have a well-known brand name and a list of loyal biscuit customers it could point at the cafés?
steps.right: Yes, it already has a brand and customer base to use
steps.wrong: No, the café business starts from nothing
steps.hint: Think about what the firm built up in its original business, and whether that asset can be pointed at a new one.

steps.q: Could the firm use that existing brand and customer base to promote the café's menu and boost café sales?
steps.right: Yes, it can use them to boost sales elsewhere
steps.wrong: No, brand and customers only work in the original market
steps.hint: If people already trust the biscuit brand, would that trust carry over when it appears on a café menu?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Biscuits and insurance use completely different factories, staff and supply chains. Can combining them let the firm buy ingredients in bulk or share a production line, the way two biscuit firms merging could?
steps.right: No, there is little to share between them
steps.wrong: Yes, the same cost savings apply
steps.hint: Economies of scale usually come from doing more of the same kind of thing. Are biscuits and insurance the same kind of thing?
steps.pre: Because the markets are unrelated, the firm gets

steps.q: The biscuit company's directors, who know baking and retail well, are now put in charge of running the insurance arm, a completely different market. Do they necessarily know how to run an insurance business well?
steps.right: No, they may lack the right knowledge
steps.wrong: Yes, good managers can run any business
steps.hint: Insurance has its own rules, risks and skills. Does biscuit experience prepare anyone for that?

steps.q: The same directors must now also oversee insurance and cafés alongside biscuits. Do they still have as many hours in the day to spend on each business as before?
steps.right: No, their time gets divided between the businesses
steps.wrong: Yes, their total time available stays focused on each
steps.hint: There is only so much management time. If it must now cover three unrelated businesses, what happens to the time each one gets?

steps.q: With attention divided this way, does the board still give its full focus to perfecting the biscuit business that made the firm successful?
steps.right: No, the core business gets less focus than before
steps.wrong: Yes, the core business stays the main priority
